node.label: Mark Mazower
node.date_label: Dark Continent (1998) · Hitler’s Empire (2008) · No Enchanted Palace (2009)
node.description: Historian of modern Europe and international order who questions celebratory accounts of liberal progress. Glenda Sluga’s reading of No Enchanted Palace identifies the imperial and racial assumptions carried into twentieth-century international institutions. Mazower’s later interview links global institutions to the power and interests of states, preserving the tension between universal claims and unequal political authority.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Age of… volumes (1962–1994) as a synthesis of “the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991”, praised by reviewers for range and analytical grasp and called “unashamedly Eurocentric” by Judt
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Mediated: the four volumes are unread. Guardian obituarists (2012, read in full): the series "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy". Judt (NYRB 1995, read in full): the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation, now exposed to steady criticism and revision"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (his endnote 2 defends the European focus). Black (Historein 2003–4, p. 215): "authoritative and commanding overviews of international history from the 18th century to present". Anderson (LRB 2002) quotes Hobsbawm on Interesting Times as "world history shaping that experience". At the 2014 conference (Times Higher Education report) Mazower spoke of a "golden age of historical synthesis". Counterweights: Judt's Eurocentrism remark and the existing critiques by Guha and Chakrabarty (edges 979, 917).

sources.title: Perry Anderson, “The Age of EJH,” London Review of Books 24, no. 19 (3 October 2002); review of Eric Hobsbawm, Interesting Times: A Twentieth-Century Life (Allen Lane, 2002).
sources.citation: Perry Anderson, “The Age of EJH,” London Review of Books 24, no. 19 (3 October 2002); review of Eric Hobsbawm, Interesting Times: A Twentieth-Century Life (Allen Lane, 2002).

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147 (LRB page; no pagination). The memoir is offered as the "flip side" of Age of Extremes, "not world history illustrated by the experiences of an individual, but world history shaping that experience" (Hobsbawm as quoted); "a kind of fifth volume, in more personal register, of a continuous project". On remaining in the Party after 1956 (Hobsbawm quoted): "I still belong to the tail-end of the first generation of Communists"; Anderson: "Most people would see in it evidence of an exceptional integrity and strength of character". Criticism: "His treatment of the traditions of others is much less impressive. Here a lack of generosity disfigures too many judgments" (Samuel, Thompson, the New Lefts); no "real intellectual engagement with the issues that haunted the trajectory of European Communism"; Marxism Today's role in "preparing the cult of Thatcher". On history: Hobsbawm gives "a good account of the rise of the analytic social history associated with the Annales and Past & Present … regretting its later retreat with the cultural turn of the 1980s" (Anderson's report); his thinking about the past is more original than Braudel's, to be seen in On History (Anderson's judgment). The memoir is unread.

verification.note: Complete text read for revision 1.147. The obituarists' dates and judgments: born Alexandria 9 June 1917, died 1 October 2012; Primitive Rebels (1959) "his first major work"; Labouring Men 1964; Industry and Empire 1968, "a compelling summation of much of his work on Britain and the industrial revolution"; the standard-of-living debate with R. M. Hartwell in the Economic History Review; the Age of… series 1962, 1975, 1987, 1994, which "distilled the history of the capitalist world from 1789 to 1991" and "were not conceived as a tetralogy"; On History (1997); Interesting Times (2002); Globalisation, Democracy and Terrorism (2007); How to Change the World, "a vigorous defence of Marx's continuing relevance in the aftermath of the banking collapse of 2008-10"; "In his later years he became arguably Britain's most respected historian of any kind".

sources.title: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).
sources.citation: Tony Judt, “Downhill All the Way,” New York Review of Books, 25 May 1995; review of Eric Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes: A History of the World, 1914–1991 (Pantheon, 1994).

verification.note: Complete text and endnotes read for revision 1.147 (NYRB page; no pagination). A "Hobsbawm generation" of historians who began between about 1959 and 1975; Primitive Rebels "first appeared in 1959"; Labouring Men, Industry and Empire and Captain Swing "substantially recast the economic history of Britain and the story of the British labor movement"; the trilogy's scheme "eventually became the “conventional” interpretation"; The Age of Revolution 1962, The Age of Capital 1975 ("Hobsbawm’s single greatest work"), The Age of Empire twelve years later. Hobsbawm is "by training and inclination an economic historian, and an analytical one" who "mostly avoids military or political narrative"; "though unashamedly Eurocentric, Eric Hobsbawm has a unique range" (endnote 2 defends the European focus). The "one" defect: "the categories right/left, fascist/Communist, progressive and reactionary seem to be very firmly set, and pretty much as they first presented themselves to Hobsbawm in the Thirties"; Bolshevism gets "no critical analytical attention except on its own restricted terms"; "“real socialism” in the lands between Germany and Russia merits just six pages"; nationalism "is a rather neglected subject". Verdict: "a challenging, often brilliant, and always cool and intelligent account". The Age of Extremes itself is unread. sources.title: “Hobsbawm’s contribution to academia celebrated,” Times Higher Education, 3 May 2014 (report on the conference “History after Hobsbawm”, Senate House, London, 29 April–1 May 2014).
sources.citation: “Hobsbawm’s contribution to academia celebrated,” Times Higher Education, 3 May 2014 (report on the conference “History after Hobsbawm”, Senate House, London, 29 April–1 May 2014).

verification.note: Complete report read for revision 1.147; speakers' words come through the reporter. Mark Mazower opened the conference with the first Hobsbawm Memorial Lecture and spoke of a continuing "golden age of historical synthesis"; Jan Rüger: "there is no clear boundary separating Britain and Europe in the Age of Empire"; Gareth Stedman Jones: a strong commitment to Marxism "generally mixes badly with the writing of good history", yet Hobsbawm combined it with "unending curiosity". Catherine Hall's History Workshop Journal essay (w1_hall_gendering_property_2014) began as a lecture at this conference.
